title: Zen, closed
hookLine: posture, poem, platform, ox, koan, bowl

lines: CUSHION, VERSE, SEAT, OX, QUESTION, BOWL.
cards: Six things on a table. A round cushion. A sheet of paper with a verse brushed on it.
A raised wooden seat where a teacher once spoke. A small painting of an ox. A slip of paper with a question on it.
And an empty bowl. Each opened a door in these weeks of Zen and Chan. Today they sit side by side, and then we do the one thing all six keep pointing back to.
Today's word, one last time in this block: Zen.

teach.b: Start with the cushion and the verse. The cushion is posture: back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered, breath allowed to be itself.
The verse is the old story of a poem on a monastery wall, answered by Huineng, a worker pounding rice in the back who could not read.
Then the seat and the ox. The seat is the platform where Huineng taught, and the sutra named after it: the nature to wake up is already here, not far off.
The ox is the set of pictures where a herdsman searches for an ox, finds it, tames it, rides it home, forgets it, and walks back into the market with open hands.
Then the question and the bowl. The question is the koan: Zhaozhou's no, three pounds of flax, the cypress, the stone bridge, a question you live with, not one you solve over coffee.
The bowl is the formal meal: bowls nested one in the next, just enough, every bowl cleaned. The ordinary task is the practice. Last, what holds all six.
Each comes back to the cushion.

teach.h: ALL SIX COME BACK TO SITTING.
teach.b: The Japanese teacher Dogen called it shikantaza, just sitting: not sitting to get calm or to crack a koan, but sitting as the whole of it.
Tomorrow a very different door opens, with a vow, a name and a land of light.

how: In Zen communities, zazen, seated meditation, is the center of practice; in the Soto school, the practice Dogen called shikantaza, just sitting, is sitting without a koan or other object.

o: a set of riddles meant to puzzle the mind
Japan's name for Chan, with sitting at the center
a feeling of calm, unbothered relaxation

p: just enough, cleaned at the end
a poem on a monastery wall

s: Zen is only about solving koans
koans are one door; all six come back to sitting, and Dogen called it just sitting.
in the ox pictures, the herdsman ends up back in the market
he forgets the ox and walks into the market with open hands.
washing up is a break from Zen practice
in the formal meal, cleaning the bowls is part of the form: the ordinary task is the practice.

games.q: after weeks of koans, poems and pictures, you ask a Zen teacher what to do next. what does the tradition keep answering?
o: wait until you feel calm enough to begin.
games.why: cushion, verse, seat, ox, question and bowl all point back to the cushion. Dogen called it just sitting.

practice: Sit: back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered or closed, with no koan, no counting, no picture to hold. When a thought comes, let it be there and let it go, the way a cloud crosses a window.

wordCard.voice: Zen. The Japanese name of the school called Chan in China: posture, verse, platform, ox, koan and bowl, and under all of them, sitting. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: zen, the reading of the Chinese chan (禪 in traditional characters), the name of the meditation school.

carryVoice: Your line: just sit. The block ends where it began, on the cushion. Until tomorrow.
